title: Control-plane routing patterns comparison: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
content:
Purpose: quick reference and concrete tradeoffs for control-plane and data-plane routing across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments. This doc is meant to capture practical patterns, operational tradeoffs, and an action-oriented rollout checklist for engineers and SREs building tenant routing and isolation for Redwood Inference.

Scope and assumptions:
- Focus: routing policy surface, isolation boundary definitions, multi-region control plane replication, and tenant affinity behavior.
- Assumes platform runtime supports configurable model variants, per-tenant version pins, and KV/prefix caching at the data-plane layer.
- Does not deeply cover billing or token accounting; see billing matrix doc for that.

Definitions: (short)
- Control plane: configuration, routing decisions, model selection and rollouts, policy evaluation.
- Data plane: actual inference endpoints handling requests and performing compute.
- Isolation boundary: degree to which tenant data and control signals are separated (network, storage, metadata).
- Routing policy: evaluation rules that choose a destination (region, capacity tier, model variant, fallback).

High-level patterns (one-liners):
- Hosted: centralized control plane, multi-tenant data-plane pools, strong runtime efficiency via shared caches and batching; isolation via logical tenancy and per-request encryption, fallbacks to cheaper regions/models.
- Dedicated: per-customer reserved pools for data plane, centralized or semi-local control plane depending on SLAs; stronger runtime isolation with predictable throughput.
- Private: control plane may be customer-managed or hybrid; data plane sits inside customer network (VPC or on-prem); routing decisions often constrained by network topology and offline sync to Redwood control plane.

Comparison matrix (practical attributes):
- Control plane locus:
  Hosted: centralized, global. Fast global policy pushes, immediate rollouts.
  Dedicated: centralized control plane for convenience, optional delegated control plane for customers with strict separation.
  Private: typically split: local control plane (customer) for runtime-critical policies + occasional sync to Redwood for billing/updates.

- Data-plane tenancy:
  Hosted: strong multiplexing (shared GPUs) with software-enforced isolation (namespaces, KV encryption). High statistical multiplexing = lower cost.
  Dedicated: tenant-dedicated pools. No noisy neighbor on GPUs; capacity reserved.
  Private: tenant owns or controls compute; isolation is physical/network.

- Routing resolution time / consistency:
  Hosted: near-real-time pushes from centralized control plane; global config consistency expected within seconds.
  Dedicated: similar to hosted if control plane is central; if delegated control plane exists, may have eventual consistency between local and global records.
  Private: often eventual consistency. Network partition or air-gapped customers introduce longer reconciliation windows.

- Rollout semantics / safety:
  Hosted: can do cross-tenant canaries and fast rollbacks; supports automatic fallbacks to compatible models across regions.
  Dedicated: rollouts commonly per-customer; canaries are customer-scoped. Fallback policies may be restricted to tenant's reserved variants.
  Private: rollouts must respect customer change windows and may require manual approval; automatic fallbacks are limited by on-prem availability.

- Networking / ingress patterns:
  Hosted: global ingress endpoints + edge routing (CDN / load-balancer) with SNI/ALPN to route tenant traffic.
  Dedicated: typically uses private peering or dedicated VPC endpoints; edge still present for public customers.
  Private: customers expose ingress inside VPC or on-prem; routing often via internal load balancers or service mesh.

- Authentication and identity propagation:
  Hosted: Redwood-issued tokens, short-lived credentials, tenant IDs in request headers. Centralized auth allows token introspection and policy gating.
  Dedicated: tokens may be scoped to tenant pools; SRE/admins can create cross-tenant infra tokens for ops.
  Private: customers often integrate their own IDP; Redwood must support federated identity or customer-managed tokens.

- KV/prefix cache locality and correctness:
  Hosted: caches are shared and designed for multi-tenant correctness (namespace keys). Benefit from larger hit-rates because of aggregated workload. Cache eviction strategies must be tenant-aware.
  Dedicated: cache locality per-customer increases hit rate for high-volume tenants; eviction easier to reason about.
  Private: caches live with customer runtime; caching strategy depends on customer topology. Cache warmup and model pinning matter more.

Failure and degradation behavior (common failure modes and recommended patterns):
- Global control plane outage:
  Hosted: have read-only cached policies at the edge and default fallback rules (route to last-known-good model variant or enter degraded mode with smaller context).
  Dedicated: local config cache on the customer pool should allow continued serving for N minutes-hours; require explicit staleness policy.
  Private: must design for offline mode; critical to provide clear staleness TTLs and observable health signals for customer SREs.

- Data-plane capacity exhaustion:
  Hosted: automatic overflow routing to lower-cost regions or model variants; throttling or queued admission.
  Dedicated: burst capacity options or pre-agreed overflow to hosted pools. Need clear billing triggers.
  Private: usually capacity-limited; recommend queued admission and operator notifications.

- Network partition (between control plane and private data plane):
  - Provide a minimal policy set that can be executed locally (fail-closed vs fail-open policy decision).
  - For private/on-prem customers, include an explicit sync protocol and conflict resolution policy in onboarding.

Routing policy examples (concrete):
1) Tenant-affinity + model-pin (Hosted)
   - Step 1: Edge receives request with tenant_id and model_pin header.
   - Step 2: Central routing policy maps tenant -> best pool (region, capacity tier) based on latency SLO and cost target.
   - Step 3: If preferred pool is saturated, fallback to sibling pool in next-lowest cost region (with explicit model-compatibility check).
   - Observability: emit chosen_pool, latency_budget, fallback_reason.

2) Dedicated with overflow to hosted
   - Primary: route to tenant's dedicated pool.
   - If queue_length > threshold or sustained CPU/GPU busy, redirect new requests to pre-configured hosted overflow pool with tenant-specific namespace.
   - Billing: mark overflow requests for per-token cross-charge.

3) Private with local control-plane enforcement
   - Customer local control-plane evaluates routing policy using local metrics.
   - If model version not present locally, local control-plane consults cached mapping to Redwood mirrors (if allowed) or returns explicit error advising operator action.

Operational recommendations (practical checklist):
- For hosted rollouts:
  - Always have a last-known-good policy bundle cached at edges.
  - Include an automatic downgrade path (functionally compatible but cheaper model) for capacity pressure.
  - Maintain per-tenant telemetry (token-level and per-route) to detect regressions early.

- For dedicated customers:
  - Provide clear contracts for overflow: API, throttling, and billing.
  - Offer delegated control plane for security-conscious customers; document consistency and SLA tradeoffs.
  - Implement tenant-aware queueing and priority adjustment for internal ops.

- For private deployments:
  - Provide an explicit offline mode spec: which policies, TTLs, and data are replicated locally.
  - Harden the sync-and-reconcile protocol; include cryptographic signing for bundle integrity.
  - Give customers tooling to validate their local routing decisions against Redwood's reference simulator before enabling in prod.

SLO and observability implications:
- Metrics to expose across environments: route_choice, control_plane_sync_age, model_variant_used, fallback_count, overflow_count, request_latency_p50/p95/p99 by region/pool.
- Alerting knobs: stale_policy_notice (> config_ttl), high_fallback_rate (> baseline), excessive_control_plane_error_rate, cache_miss_ratio (tenant-specific).

Security and compliance notes:
- Hosted: must ensure tenant-level encryption of cached KV and model context. RBAC for rollout triggers. Maintain audit trails for model pin changes.
- Dedicated: restrict cross-tenant telemetry in mixed pools. For dedicated pools with shared infra, ensure rate-limited access to control plane metadata.
- Private: certify the sync protocol for customers with high compliance needs. Include options for HSM-backed signing of bundles, private CA for mutual TLS.

Decision guidance (quick heuristics):
- Choose Hosted if: many small tenants, cost-sensitivity, need for fast rollouts and global fallbacks.
- Choose Dedicated if: predictable throughput, need for SLAs, strong performance isolation.
- Choose Private if: regulatory/data residency concerns, on-prem requirements, or customer insists on network isolation.

Migration checklist (Hosted -> Dedicated or Dedicated -> Private):
- Inventory: list tenant model pins, cache warmup artifacts, affinity metadata, and data retention rules.
- Policy freeze window: schedule a short freeze during DNS and ingress changes.
- Warmup: proactively populate KV/prefix caches in target pools and validate model weights availability.
- Traffic cutover plan: staged weighted rollouts followed by monitoring for fallback metrics.

Open questions / tradeoffs for follow-up:
- How aggressively should hosted pools share KV caches for low-sensitivity tenants? (privacy vs efficiency)
- Delegated control plane: what subset of policies is safe to transfer to customer-managed control plane without losing global observability?
- Cost accounting for overflow: best practices for per-token attribution when requests traverse multiple organizational pools.

Appendix: short example of a policy bundle (pseudo-RBAC style - kept textual)
- policy_bundle version: v1
- tenant_rules:
  - tenant_id: ACME
    model_pin: rwd-7b-v2
    preferred_regions: [us-west1, us-east1]
    overflow_policy: hosted_overflow_allowed
    max_queue_latency_ms: 200

Note: this doc is intentionally operational and compact — use as a companion to the longer control-plane conops and the tenant isolation playbook.
